w: L17 · Pregnancy and Lactation Hormonal support of pregnancy and the role of the placenta/corpus luteum Said in class “This is the important part, is this last one ... this hCG ... Because this is what rescues the corpus luteum.” “hCG prevents the regression of corpus luteum, slows production of LH and FSH.” “Estradiol, just normal menstrual cycle estrogen. Estrone is menopause. Estriol is the predominant estrogen during pregnancy.” Know this hCG comes from the trophoblasts (syncytiotrophoblasts) from about 8 days after ovulation. It rescues the corpus luteum, so progesterone and estrogen stay up and LH and FSH stay low. A pregnancy test measures hCG (urine or blood, 10 to 11 days after fertilization); it peaks at about 10 weeks. First trimester: the corpus luteum makes most of the progesterone and estrogen. The placenta is fully developed by the end of the first trimester, then takes over. Progesterone readies the endometrium for implantation and keeps the uterus quiet. Without a pregnancy the corpus luteum regresses (corpus albicans) about 14 days after ovulation. The placenta makes progesterone on its own but lacks 17,20 desmolase, so estriol needs the fetus: fetal adrenal DHEA sulfate, 16-hydroxylated in the fetal liver, aromatized by the placenta. Estriol reflects fetal health. hPL (human placental lactogen): breast growth and anti-insulin actions, so pregnancy is insulin resistant (gestational diabetes). Relaxin keeps the myometrium quiet and softens the cervix. Watch for: hCG is made by the trophoblasts and acts on the corpus luteum, not the other way around. Progesterone alone, estrogen with the fetus; the 16-hydroxylation is the fetal liver. hPL is not hCG. Insulin rises in pregnancy. Hormonal changes associated with delivery and the postpartum period Said in class “I think the big one is that increased oxytocin secretion coming from the posterior ... post-delivery, these contractions continue. That helps to prevent excessive bleeding.” Know this Delivery is about 40 weeks after the last menstrual period (not after fertilization). Uterine stretch is a trigger. The estrogen-to-progesterone ratio rises: estrogen contracts, progesterone relaxes. The uterus upregulates PGF2 alpha and oxytocin receptors. PGF2 alpha contracts (more intracellular calcium); PGE2 softens and thins the cervix. Oxytocin (posterior pituitary) is the big one: contractions by positive feedback, and after delivery it keeps the uterus contracting to limit bleeding. Delivering the placenta drops progesterone, which frees prolactin: full milk production starts. Watch for: Receptors go up, not down. Don't swap the prostaglandins: PGE2 is the cervix, PGF2 alpha the contraction. After delivery oxytocin limits bleeding; it doesn't raise progesterone. Prolactin vs. oxytocin Said in class “Prolactin sets the stage and creates all the milk products. Oxytocin is going to stimulate milk letdown.” Know this Prolactin = milk production; oxytocin = milk letdown (ejection). A swap is the obvious trap. Prolactin: anterior pituitary, tonically inhibited by dopamine. With cortisol it raises the milk enzymes. Oxytocin: made in the hypothalamus, released from the posterior pituitary; contracts the myoepithelial cells around each alveolus. In pregnancy prolactin rises but is antagonized by progesterone. High prolactin inhibits GnRH. Watch for: Oxytocin squeezes milk out; it doesn't make milk or milk enzymes. Prolactin's brake is dopamine, not oxytocin or GnRH. Oxytocin isn't from the anterior pituitary or the placenta. Neuroendocrine effects of suckling Said in class “Mainly focus on this side of things. Dopamine being important.” “One thing that I want to highlight: prolactin is going to also inhibit gonadotropin-releasing hormone.” Know this Suckling lowers dopamine, so the anterior pituitary releases prolactin (prolactin releasing factor adds to it): milk production. Suckling also releases oxytocin from the posterior pituitary: the myoepithelial cells contract, letdown. High prolactin inhibits GnRH: less LH, FSH and sex steroids, so periods stop while breastfeeding (the same as hyperprolactinemia from any cause). Watch for: Suckling lowers dopamine; a choice saying it raises dopamine is wrong. Prolactin, not oxytocin, inhibits GnRH. Missing periods while breastfeeding aren't leftover hCG. Regulation of milk production and milk ejection Said in class “What you should know is that a lot of prolactin's effects during pregnancy are inhibited. They're kind of antagonized by progesterone.” Know this Pregnancy builds the breast: estrogen grows and branches the ducts (and fat); progesterone adds alveoli; prolactin and cortisol raise the milk enzymes; hPL helps. Progesterone antagonizes prolactin, so there is no full milk until delivery. The placenta out, progesterone falls, and prolactin drives full milk production. Production stays on because suckling keeps dopamine low and prolactin high. Ejection is oxytocin contracting the myoepithelial cells. Watch for: Progesterone adds alveoli; estrogen grows the ducts. Cortisol raises the milk enzymes. Full milk waits because of progesterone, not missing alveoli or placental dopamine. The questions name progesterone as the antagonist. Also stressed in class Not on the study guide, but flagged in the recording. Said in class “ZP3, when the sperm recognize that, that is oftentimes going to initiate the acrosomal reaction.” “Binding to that ZP2 protein stimulates what we call the cortical or zonal reaction ... so that you don't have more than one sperm.” Know this ZP3 on the zona pellucida sets off the acrosomal reaction; the sperm then binds ZP2. Binding ZP2 starts the oocyte's second meiotic division and the cortical (zonal) reaction, which blocks polyspermy. Implantation is at the blastocyst stage; the trophoblasts are its outer layer. The pill: its estrogen blunts the LH surge (no ovulation), its progestin thickens cervical mucus; high-dose estrogen prevents implantation. Said not needed The names of the cleavage stages, the adhesion molecules' names (L-selectin and the rest), and the methods that keep sperm and egg apart. Key terms hCG From the trophoblasts; rescues the corpus luteum, keeps LH and FSH low; the pregnancy test. progesterone Corpus luteum, then the placenta; readies the endometrium, relaxes the uterus, adds alveoli and holds prolactin back until delivery. prolactin Anterior pituitary; makes the milk; held down by dopamine; inhibits GnRH. oxytocin Hypothalamus, released from the posterior pituitary; letdown, labor contractions, limits bleeding after delivery. L18 · Estrogens and Androgens Major actions of estrogens, progestins, and androgens Said in class “Dihydrotestosterone is the active testosterone. That is the one that is active.” “Those who have aromatase deficiency are not able to make estradiol, and they're the ones that grow very tall ... they have weak bone.” Know this Cholesterol to DHEA (dehydroepiandrosterone) to androstenedione to testosterone. 5-alpha-reductase makes DHT, the active form; aromatase makes estradiol. Lipophilic, carried on SHBG; the free hormone binds a nuclear receptor and changes gene expression, so the effect takes time. Testosterone: male traits, sperm, more red cells, water and salt retention, more muscle, lower HDL, lower binding globulins. Estradiol closes the epiphyses: a man without aromatase grows very tall with weak, osteoporotic bones. Estrogen: the uterine muscle and lining, raises HDL and triglycerides, protects bone (antagonizes PTH resorption), and raises clotting factors II, VII, IX and X while lowering antithrombin III. Progesterone: the action he stressed is maturation of the endometrium. Watch for: DHEA is the precursor, not dihydrotestosterone (his slide mislabels it; he corrected it). Testosterone rides SHBG, not CBG, and lowers HDL. A man without aromatase is tall, not short. How hormonal contraceptives prevent pregnancy Said in class “Plan B has to be used within 72 hours, but ulipristal, that is your Ella, can be used up to 5 days ... ulipristal is by prescription only, whereas you can buy Plan B without prescription.” Know this Progestins activate the progestin receptor and suppress FSH (and LH): no ovulation. The combined pill adds ethinyl estradiol; levonorgestrel is the common progestin. Can't take estrogen (a clot history, breast or uterine cancer): a progestin-only pill. Of ethinyl estradiol, estradiol, estrone and levonorgestrel, the least estrogenic is levonorgestrel. Plan B = high-dose levonorgestrel, within 72 hours, no prescription. Ulipristal (Ella) = a progestin receptor antagonist, up to 5 days, prescription only. Mifepristone blocks the progestin and glucocorticoid receptors: not in Addison disease. Progestin cautions: hypertension, lower HDL, pregnancy wanted soon. Watch for: Progestins activate the receptor; ulipristal and mifepristone block it. Plan B is levonorgestrel, not ethinyl estradiol or ulipristal, and its window is 72 hours, not 24. Major drug classes that alter reproductive hormone signaling Said in class “The names will suggest to you how they work, based on their classes, like aromatase inhibitors, so you know they inhibit aromatase enzyme.” “Tamoxifen for breast cancer, raloxifene for osteoporosis, Clomid, that is for, to stimulate ovulation.” “Pay attention to those drugs that I highlight in the slides, and you should be fine.” Know this Androgens: testosterone and testosterone cypionate (the IM depot); DHEA (prasterone) is over the counter. GnRH analogs (goserelin, leuprolide): constant stimulation instead of pulses switches the pituitary off, so FSH, LH and testosterone fall. Prostate cancer mainly. Estrogens: estradiol (replacement), ethinyl estradiol (the pill), estrone (Premarin, menopause). SERMs: tamoxifen blocks the breast, stimulates the uterus, only for ER-positive breast cancer; raloxifene for osteoporosis, no uterine stimulation; clomiphene blocks estrogen's negative feedback so LH and FSH rise: ovulation. Aromatase inhibitors (anastrozole): block testosterone to estradiol, for breast cancer. Watch for: Anastrozole blocks the enzyme; tamoxifen blocks the receptor. Goserelin works by never pausing, not by blocking a receptor. Premarin is estrone. Skip the other androgen analogs and the rarely used SERMs. Drugs that block androgen receptors or androgen metabolism Said in class “The difference between Proscar and Propecia is the dose, the strength of the tablet. And also for the indication. The high strength is for BPH, the low strength is for alopecia.” Know this 5-alpha-reductase inhibitors (finasteride, dutasteride) block testosterone to DHT. Uses: BPH and hair loss. Side effects: gynecomastia, sexual dysfunction. Proscar and Propecia are both finasteride: higher strength for BPH, lower for hair loss. His dental case: low libido and breast tenderness on finasteride. Androgen receptor antagonists (flutamide, bicalutamide) compete at the receptor: prostate cancer, excess androgens in women. Side effects: GI upset (least with bicalutamide), gynecomastia, hepatotoxicity. Gynecomastia is on all three anti-androgen lists (with the GnRH analogs). Watch for: Finasteride blocks 5-alpha-reductase, not the receptor or aromatase. The enzyme that activates testosterone is 5-alpha-reductase (aromatase makes estradiol). Bicalutamide causes the least GI upset. Important therapeutic effects and adverse effects Said in class “I think the most important side effect of testosterone everyone needs to also know is hepatotoxicity.” “I think it's the most serious and most common side effect of estrogens.” “At least you should be able to remember hot flashes associated with estrogens and thromboembolism.” Know this Testosterone: hepatotoxicity; liver disease rules it out. Avoid in BPH, pregnancy, breast or prostate cancer in men. Women: hirsutism, a deep voice; men: gynecomastia (from estradiol), sleep apnea. Estrogens: thromboembolism, the most serious and most common side effect (more clotting factors, less antithrombin III). Any clot or stroke, breast cancer or pregnancy rules them out. They make warfarin work less well. SERMs share the clot risk: raloxifene raises DVT and PE 2 to 3 times (his case: a clot while immobile after an extraction); tamoxifen adds uterine cancer. Clomiphene: multiple births, ovarian cysts. Aromatase inhibitors: hot flashes and thromboembolism; not before menopause. Adding progesterone to menopause estrogen cuts the uterine cancer risk. Progestins: hypertension, lower HDL. Watch for: Androgens lower HDL. Hirsutism is an androgen effect, not an estrogen one. Estrogen weakens warfarin. Raloxifene's dental risk is a clot. Case 1's pregnancy answer is testosterone. Said not needed The other androgen analogs on his table, the rest of the second estrogen-effects slide (ACTH, well-being, binding globulins), and the rarely used SERMs (toremifene, ospemifene, bazedoxifene, fulvestrant). Key terms GnRH analogs Goserelin, leuprolide: constant stimulation shuts off FSH, LH and testosterone; prostate cancer. progestins Activate the progestin receptor, suppress FSH and LH: no ovulation. Levonorgestrel, Plan B. antiandrogens Three ways: GnRH analogs (production), 5-alpha-reductase inhibitors (activation to DHT), receptor antagonists (flutamide, bicalutamide). Gynecomastia in all. 5α-reductase inhibitors Finasteride, dutasteride: block testosterone to DHT; BPH and hair loss; gynecomastia, sexual dysfunction. L19 · Introduction to Hematology Recognition and major functions of RBCs, platelets, and leukocytes Said in class “What you need to remember with white blood cells is we've got two classes and 5 types.” “Remember, platelets arise from megakaryocytes. That's just knowledge you should know.” Know this Red cells (about 99 percent of blood cells) carry oxygen and carbon dioxide. Platelets are pieces of megakaryocytes in the bone marrow and start clotting. Granulocytes (prominent granules): neutrophils, eosinophils, basophils. Agranulocytes: monocytes and lymphocytes (B, T, NK). Most to least common: neutrophils (50 to 70%), lymphocytes (30 to 40%), monocytes, eosinophils, basophils (under 1%): Never Let Monkeys Eat Bananas. Nuclei: neutrophil multi-lobed; eosinophil and basophil bilobed; monocyte one large indented (horseshoe) nucleus; lymphocyte big and round. NK cells are the large lymphocytes. One stem cell, two lines: lymphoid (B and T cells) and myeloid (red cells, megakaryocytes, granulocytes, monocytes). In an adult every blood cell comes from the marrow. Watch for: Platelets are made in the marrow, not the spleen (the spleen stores a third of them). The monocyte is myeloid even without granules. Functions of neutrophils, eosinophils, basophils, monocytes, and lymphocytes Said in class “So you know that term, plasma cell. And you can associate that with antibody production and release.” Know this Neutrophil: the main phagocyte, first line against bacteria; about 10 hours in the blood. Granules with elastase and myeloperoxidase. Eosinophil: parasites and allergy (hay fever); major basic protein disrupts parasite membranes; IgE receptors. Basophil: heparin and histamine, released when IgE binds; asthma. Monocyte: about 3 days in the blood, then becomes the macrophage; phagocytoses and presents antigen on MHC class II. Lymphocytes: B cells (become antibody-making plasma cells), T cells (help or kill), NK cells (kill altered cells). Watch for: 10 hours is the neutrophil, 3 days the monocyte. Eosinophils and basophils are both bilobed with IgE receptors: the granules tell them apart. The monocyte becomes the macrophage, not the plasma cell. Innate vs. adaptive immunity Said in class “Just think when you hear the word humoral, think B-cell response, okay? And then also, when you hear B cells, think about the production of antibodies.” Know this Innate (nonspecific, ready before contact): barriers (skin, mucosa), low pH, lysozyme, thiocyanate in saliva, interferons, phagocytes and NK cells. Adaptive (specific): built by B and T cells after a first contact with an antigen; often leaves memory. Humoral = B cells and antibodies. Cellular = T cells, against virus-infected and transformed cells. Watch for: Antibodies are adaptive, never innate. Thiocyanate is innate. NK cells are lymphocytes but innate; the killer T cells of adaptive immunity are the CD8 cells. General roles of B cells, T cells, and NK cells Said in class “It's just, in general speaking, kind of what NK cells are doing in three different scenarios.” “The helper T cells are what's going to help our B lymphocytes, and the cytotoxic T cells are probably just gonna kill whatever they bind.” Know this B cells: surface IgM and IgD; with T cell help they become plasma cells that release antibody. T cells: the TCR sees antigen only on MHC. CD4 helpers see MHC class II and help B cells; CD8 cytotoxic cells see MHC class I and kill with perforins. (4 times 2 and 8 times 1 both make 8.) NK cells: large, innate, no B or T markers, no antigen receptor (CD16, CD56). Healthy cell (MHC class I binds the inhibitory receptor): spared. Missing MHC class I: killed. Far more activating ligands: induced killing. ADCC: antibody coats the target; the NK cell's CD16 binds IgG's constant region; perforins and granzymes kill. No TCR, no MHC. Watch for: Perforins are the CD8 cell's (and NK's), not the helper's. Only T cells need antigen on MHC. NK cells check MHC class I (he once said class 2). Primary vs. secondary lymphoid organs Said in class “We're not going to consider GALT as a primary lymphatic organ, but we will consider the thymus and the bone marrow as our primary lymphoid organs.” “Epithelioreticular cells, you should associate that with the thymus.” Know this Primary: bone marrow and thymus only. They make lymphocytes immunocompetent before antigen: B and NK cells in the marrow (self-reactive B cells removed there), T cells in the thymus. Secondary: lymph nodes (filter lymph), MALT and GALT (tonsils, Peyer's patches in the ileum, appendix; IgA) and the spleen (filters blood). Antigen meets lymphocytes there and they proliferate. Stroma: reticular cells and reticulin (type III collagen) everywhere except the thymus, which has epithelioreticular cells. Tonsils (Waldeyer's ring): pharyngeal (adenoids; a child's adenoiditis means mouth breathing), tubal, palatine (crypts), lingual. No afferent lymphatics. Watch for: GALT, tonsils and Peyer's patches are secondary. Reticulin is type III collagen, not type I. Self-reactive B cells go in the marrow, not the thymus. Basic organization and function of the thymus, lymph node, and spleen Said in class “There's a lot of programmed cell death that occurs as a process of thymocyte selection. So approximately 95 to 99% of the cells that go there are going to be selected out.” “The main thing is just to really associate this PALS with the spleen.” Know this Thymus: behind the manubrium; largest in the newborn, involutes to fat by the teens. Dark cortex (packed T cells, positive selection), light medulla (negative selection, Hassall's corpuscles). 95 to 99% of thymocytes die. They leave CD4 or CD8 positive. The blood-thymus barrier shields them. Lymph node: cortex = B cell follicles (a secondary follicle has a germinal center), paracortex = T cells (high endothelial venules), medulla = plasma cells secreting antibody. Lymph in by afferent, out by efferent lymphatics: the only one with both. Spleen: filters blood; no afferent lymphatics. White pulp: the PALS of T cells around the central arteriole, B cell nodules, the marginal zone. Red pulp (most of it): cords and sinusoids, where it clears old red cells and platelets and recycles iron. Type Primary Secondary Secondary Job Trains T cells Filters lymph Filters blood Lymphatics Efferent only Afferent and efferent Efferent only B cells Not its job Cortex follicles White pulp nodules T cells Cortex, then medulla Paracortex PALS Landmark Hassall's corpuscles High endothelial venules Central arteriole with its PALS Watch for: PALS means spleen and T cells. A primary follicle has no germinal center. The spleen has white and red pulp, not a cortex and medulla. Old red cells are the spleen's job, not the node's. Said not needed Stained images (none on the exam), the cell counts per liter, the long list of lymphoid tissues, the colony-forming unit names, and how helper and cytotoxic T cells respond differently. Key terms neutrophil The most common white cell, multi-lobed; first line against bacteria. eosinophil Bilobed, red granules; major basic protein; parasites and allergy. NK cell Large innate lymphocyte, no B or T markers; kills cells missing MHC class I; CD16 for ADCC. thymus Primary organ for T cells; epithelioreticular stroma; cortex positive, medulla negative selection; involutes. bone marrow Primary organ; every adult blood cell; B and NK cells mature there. spleen Secondary organ that filters blood; white pulp and red pulp; clears old red cells. PALS T cells around the central arteriole of the spleen's white pulp. L20 · Lymphomas and Leukemias How the major leukemias are classified Said in class “If you see greater than 20% blast, you can go ahead and diagnose an acute leukemia ... That's our threshold for making the diagnosis.” Know this Two axes: acute (blasts that don't mature) or chronic (cells still mature); myeloid (granulocytes, monocytes) or lymphoid (B and T cells). Four leukemias: AML, ALL, CML, CLL. More than 20 percent blasts in blood or marrow = acute leukemia (an AML with a defining genetic abnormality at any count). Blasts in the blood are always abnormal, except in newborns. Leukemia lives in the marrow and blood; lymphoma generally in the nodes. Workup: blood count, smear, then a marrow aspirate and biopsy (posterior iliac crest). MDS: lasting low counts, abnormal-looking precursors, blasts under 20 percent; it can become AML. Watch for: CLL is lymphoid. ALL, not AML, is the acute leukemia of young children. Low counts with 8 percent blasts is MDS, not AML. The number is 20. Acute vs. chronic disease Said in class “The main chronic leukemia that you need to know is chronic myeloid leukemia.” Know this Acute: rapid, under 6 months untreated, blasts over 20%, platelets low, mild organomegaly. CML: insidious, 2 to 6 years, mature cells (blasts under 20%), a very high white count with neutrophils at every stage, platelets normal or high early, a big spleen. Both end in infection or bleeding. CML: t(9;22), the Philadelphia chromosome, BCR-ABL1, a kinase always on; imatinib blocks it. Most found in the chronic phase; untreated, a blast phase follows. CLL/SLL: one disease of small mature B cells (blood = CLL, node = SLL); age 70 or older; smudge cells, soccer-ball chromatin; infections from hypogammaglobulinemia; slow but largely incurable. Watch for: Mostly mature cells with under 20 percent blasts is chronic, not acute. CML's onset is insidious. SLL is not a different disease. Myeloid vs. lymphoid disease Said in class “Two big ones you need to know. Acute promyelocytic leukemia, which is associated with translocation 15 and 17.” Know this AML: adults (median 65); medium to large blasts with granules, distinct nucleoli, maybe Auer rods. ALL: children 1 to 5; small blasts, scant cytoplasm, no granules. Auer rods mean myeloid: never ALL. B-ALL is the most common childhood leukemia (over 90 percent long-term remission); T-ALL often has a mediastinal mass. Only their demographics are needed. APL: t(15;17), PML-RARA; stuck at the promyelocyte; bundles of Auer rods. Acute monocytic leukemia: kidney-shaped nuclei; it can show in the gums. Myeloid disease: AML, CML, MDS. Lymphoid: ALL, CLL/SLL, the lymphomas, myeloma. Watch for: Lymphoblasts never carry granules or Auer rods. Retinoic acid matures APL's cells; imatinib blocks CML's kinase. Major differences between Hodgkin and non-Hodgkin lymphoma Said in class “That's the main thing that you need to recognize, is those Hodgkin and Reed-Sternberg cells.” “Some key symptoms, that are called B symptoms, that are really, like, high-yield clues.” Know this Hodgkin: localized, central nodes above the diaphragm, spreads contiguously node to node, extranodal uncommon, blood never; over 80 percent cured. Non-Hodgkin (mostly B-cell): widespread, peripheral or extranodal, can skip node groups, can involve the blood. Reed-Sternberg cells: few, very large, two lobes with pink nucleoli (owl's eye) in a reactive crowd. EBV drives some cases. B symptoms: fever of 38 °C or more, drenching night sweats, 10 percent weight loss in 6 months. The tissue makes the diagnosis. Disseminated (marrow, liver) = stage 4. Watch for: Hodgkin doesn't involve the blood or usually start outside the nodes. Bone pain isn't a B symptom. A starry sky is Burkitt. Skip the Hodgkin subtypes. Recognizing important lymphoma categories and associations Said in class “I want you to know generally kind of what category things are ... You do need to know the molecular associations on the ones that are sort of underlined.” “Let's say this is expressing cyclin D1. You would know this is mantle cell lymphoma.” “Starry sky pattern is the key morphologic finding in making this diagnosis.” “The last low-grade B-cell lymphoma is the one you guys are going to experience the most. Marginal zone lymphoma.” Know this 85 to 90 percent are B-cell. Indolent B: CLL/SLL, follicular, mantle cell, marginal zone. Aggressive B: DLBCL, Burkitt. T-cell: mycosis fungoides (indolent), Sézary, peripheral T-cell, NK/T (aggressive). Follicular: t(14;18), BCL2 on, the cells don't die; widespread but often no symptoms. Mantle cell: t(11;14), cyclin D1: nothing else does that. Marginal zone (MALT): indolent, from chronic inflammation: stomach H. pylori, ocular adnexa Chlamydia psittaci, salivary gland Sjögren, thyroid Hashimoto; lymphoepithelial lesions. Burkitt: very aggressive; t(8;14), MYC; starry sky; endemic in African children's jaw, EBV. DLBCL: sheets of large cells, a fast-growing mass. Mycosis fungoides: the most common skin lymphoma, T-cell, patches then plaques then tumors. Sézary syndrome, its aggressive form: erythroderma, nodes, Sézary cells in the blood. Multiple myeloma: an M-spike, CRAB (high calcium, renal, anemia, lytic bone), rouleaux. t(14;18) BCL2, IGH Follicular t(11;14) Cyclin D1, IGH Mantle cell t(8;14) MYC, IGH Burkitt t(9;22) BCR-ABL1 CML t(15;17) PML-RARA APL Watch for: Each translocation's distractors are the other four. Mantle cell is the mantle zone, not the marginal zone. Skip the CD markers and flow cytometry. Common clinical consequences of leukemia Said in class “Sometimes these leukemias can actually present as gingival hypertrophy and oral lesion. So you guys may actually be the clue that a patient has leukemia that's not detected.” Know this Marrow failure: anemia (pallor, fatigue), low platelets (bruising, bleeding gums, petechiae), too few working white cells (fever, infections). Organ infiltration: bone pain, a big spleen, liver and nodes, CNS signs, gingival hypertrophy. Swollen gums with fatigue, pallor and bruising: get a blood count (acute monocytic leukemia infiltrates the gums). APL: DIC, which can kill early; all-trans retinoic acid with arsenic trioxide largely cures it. Untreated leukemia is fatal by infection or bleeding; the goal is complete remission. Watch for: Gingival hypertrophy is infiltration, not marrow failure: the EXCEPT. Swollen leukemic gums are leukemic cells, not plaque gingivitis. APL's emergency is DIC. Said not needed The CD markers and flow cytometry (“Do not waste a second learning what these antigens are”), the AML subtypes (M0 to M7) and subtype lists, the Hodgkin subtypes, and peripheral T-cell lymphoma past its gist (very aggressive, B symptoms). Key terms ALL Acute lymphoblastic: children 1 to 5; small blasts, never Auer rods. AML Acute myeloid: adults; over 20 percent blasts; Auer rods; APL and acute monocytic. CLL Small mature B cells (= SLL); 70 or older; smudge cells; hypogammaglobulinemia. CML t(9;22), BCR-ABL1; very high count at every stage; big spleen; imatinib. Reed-Sternberg cells The owl's-eye cells of classic Hodgkin, few among reactive cells. Burkitt lymphoma t(8;14), MYC; starry sky; African children's jaw, EBV. Mantle cell lymphoma t(11;14), cyclin D1; the mantle zone. Mycosis fungoides/Sézary syndrome Indolent skin T-cell lymphoma; Sézary is its aggressive form with erythroderma and blood cells. L21 · Male Reproductive and Lower Urinary Tract Pathology Disorders of testicular development/descent Said in class “Those high temperatures halt the spermatogenesis, and can be the cause of infertility and testicular cancer ... Even if it's surgically corrected, infertility won't occur, but the risk of testicular cancer is still a possibility for that kid.” “Two conditions, benign conditions in the testis that are relatively frequent, and both are medical emergencies.” Know this Cryptorchidism (“crypto means hidden”): a testis left in the retroperitoneum or inguinal canal. The slide: about 3 percent of full-term and 30 percent of premature boys. The scrotum keeps the testis about 2 degrees cool. At body temperature heat halts spermatogenesis: infertility and testicular cancer (seminoma by name). Surgery by about 2 years prevents the infertility, but the cancer risk stays. The two emergencies: testicular torsion (a twisted cord, the testis infarcts; veins close first) and inguinal hernia (bowel trapped in an open canal; bowel sounds over the mass). A hydrocele (fluid in the tunica vaginalis) is not one. Hypospadias: the urethra opens underneath (ventral); epispadias: on top (dorsal). Watch for: Heat halts spermatogenesis; it doesn't speed it up. After surgery the risk that stays is cancer, not infertility. Major categories of testicular tumors Said in class “95% of the testicular tumors are derived from the spermatogonias, the germ cell tumors. And the rest are derived from the Sertoli cells, the Leydig cells, what we call sex cord-stromal tumors.” “Seminoma behaves very well and responds to radiotherapy. The rest of the tumors in the testicle won't respond so well.” Know this 95 percent are germ cell tumors (from spermatogonia), cured in more than 95 percent. The rest: sex cord-stromal (Sertoli and Leydig cell tumors), mixed, and in older men secondary lymphoma and metastases. Risk: cryptorchidism (also a prior testicular cancer, family history); peak in the 20s. Seminoma, the most frequent: young adults, 30s and 40s; white, solid, multinodular, no hemorrhage or necrosis; usually no serum marker; behaves very well, responds to radiotherapy. Non-seminomatous: embryonal carcinoma, yolk sac tumor, choriocarcinoma, teratoma: more aggressive, less radiosensitive. Watch for: Sertoli and Leydig cell tumors are never germ cell tumors. A young adult with a white, solid tumor and no marker has a seminoma. Common infections of the male reproductive tract Said in class “The lower numbers, 6 and 11, are benign. Higher numbers, 16 and 18, are premalignant ... 30% evolve to invasive carcinomas if they are not treated.” Know this Glans and foreskin (balanoposthitis): nonspecific bacteria, or syphilis, gonorrhea, chlamydia. Epididymitis: usually a spreading UTI or prostatitis; under 35, gonorrhea or chlamydia. Orchitis is very uncommon (rarer than epididymitis): mumps, syphilis, tuberculosis, brucellosis. HPV 6 and 11: condyloma acuminatum, benign, verrucous, very contagious. HPV 16 and 18: PeIN, flat and red, premalignant; about 30 percent of the HPV-associated kind become invasive untreated. The HPV-independent kind: older uncircumcised men with lichen sclerosus. Phimosis (a foreskin that can't retract): smegma, infection, chronic inflammation, penile carcinoma. Watch for: Orchitis is the rare one. Condyloma doesn't lead to carcinoma; 16 and 18 do. Phimosis predisposes to penile carcinoma, cryptorchidism to testicular cancer: don't swap them. Major benign and malignant prostate disorders Said in class “These two zones can predict the pathology. The benign prostatic hyperplasia is located around the urethra ... and the peripheral zone is the location of the prostatic carcinomas.” “Guys, you are going to have it. You cannot avoid this.” “It likes to metastasize in bones, and that bone metastasis characteristically forms more bone ... We are going to order a blood draw for PSA.” Know this BPH: glands and stroma around the urethra (transition zone), in nearly every man after 50; it obstructs the urine; surgery for severe cases. Not taught as a precursor of cancer. Prostatic adenocarcinoma: the most frequent cancer in men, over 65; in the peripheral zone, so no early obstruction. Found by serum PSA (also follows recurrence). It likes bone: osteoblastic metastases. An osteoblastic lesion in a man: think prostate, order a PSA. Gleason grades differentiation (well-formed glands to masses and single cells): worse differentiation, worse prognosis. Watch for: Don't swap the zones. Gleason grades differentiation, not depth (depth stages bladder cancer). Painless hematuria points to the bladder, not the prostate. So smoking is a very strong risk factor for urothelial carcinoma.” Know this 90 percent of urinary tract tumors are urothelial carcinomas, most in the bladder; painless hematuria is the sign. Smoking: four times the risk, and quitting doesn't lower it (unlike lung cancer). Others: dyes, rubber, leather; pelvic radiation; cyclophosphamide; chronic catheters; Schistosoma haematobium (squamous cell carcinoma). Low versus high grade (nuclear pleomorphism); the depth of invasion sets the stage. Bladder cancer is fourth in incidence in men (the slide). Ureteral obstruction: stones (at the narrow spots, especially where the ureter enters the bladder) and tumors. Vagina: vaginitis is its most frequent condition (Candida, Trichomonas, atrophic). Tumors: VaIN and squamous cell carcinoma; sarcoma botryoides in girls under 5. Lichen simplex chronicus: thick, leathery skin from scratching. Lichen sclerosus: atrophic epithelium over dermal sclerosis, smooth like parchment; it leads to the HPV-independent vulvar squamous cell carcinoma of women over 60. Lichen planus: vulvar and oral lesions together, white and lace-like, painful erosions; a fresh biopsy (not formalin) for immunofluorescence; steroids. Vulvar squamous cell carcinoma: HPV-associated (HPV 16 in more than 70 percent) or HPV-independent (older women, lichen sclerosus; the slide adds lichen planus). Lichen sclerosus's carcinoma is the HPV-independent one. Distinguishing neoplastic from non-neoplastic lesions Know this Non-neoplastic: vaginitis (Candida, Trichomonas, atrophic), the three lichens, chronic endometritis, mastitis, duct ectasia, fat necrosis. Neoplastic: the cervix's squamous intraepithelial lesions (CIN), VaIN, squamous cell carcinoma, sarcoma botryoides, leiomyoma (benign) and leiomyosarcoma. In situ stays in the epithelium; invading the stroma makes it squamous cell carcinoma. Non-neoplastic isn't always harmless: lichen sclerosus is inflammatory yet leads to carcinoma. Condyloma (HPV 6 and 11) is benign. Breast, as taught: DCIS needs treatment; the WHO now calls LCIS neoplastic but benign, no treatment. Paget disease of the nipple means a carcinoma beneath. Watch for: In “select the neoplastic lesions” the decoys are atrophic vaginitis, Candida vaginitis and lichen simplex chronicus. The questions follow the lecture on LCIS. Important infectious causes of reproductive tract disease Said in class “Candida, like this, pseudohyphae, what we can see here as little sticks ... Trichomonas vaginalis is a protozoan that is very easy to diagnose in cytology, because it looks like a squamous cell, but it has a prolongation.” Know this Candida (fungus): pseudohyphae, “little sticks”, lots of inflammation. Trichomonas vaginalis: a sexually transmitted protozoan; a squamous-looking cell with cytoplasmic prolongations. Atrophic vaginitis: older women, not an infection. HPV: 6 and 11 cause condyloma; 16 and 18 the squamous intraepithelial lesions and carcinomas. Its mark: the koilocyte. Chronic endometritis: plasma cells in the endometrium; a common, easily treated cause of infertility (antibiotics). Mastitis: breastfeeding, skin bacteria, antibiotics. Watch for: Prolongations are Trichomonas, little sticks Candida, a halo around the nucleus HPV. The lichens are inflammatory, not infectious. Relationship between HPV and cervical neoplasia Said in class “That transformation zone is very important as a localization of the endocervical cancer, or the cervical cancer.” “Low-grade have a low progression and can regress. The high grade are less likely to regress and can more likely progress to carcinomas.” “The cell is called the koilocyte, because it has a cavity in the middle.” Know this The transformation zone: the “fighting of epithelia” keeps it inflamed and open to HPV, so cervical cancer arises there. Precursors: squamous intraepithelial lesions. Low grade (CIN1) can regress; high grade (CIN2, CIN3) progresses. About 90 percent HPV-linked, types 16 and 18. Koilocyte: a bigger nucleus in a clear halo, what the Pap smear looks for. High grade: less cytoplasm, high N:C ratio, pleomorphic nuclei. Pap screening lowers U.S. incidence and deaths; the vaccine lowers incidence, its full benefit decades away. Screening is now risk-based. Watch for: Low grade regresses, high grade progresses. HPV 6 and 11 don't cause the high-grade lesions. Screening, not the vaccine, explains the lower U.S. rate. Reproductive age: squamous cell carcinomas of the cervix and vagina (HPV). Endometrioid adenocarcinoma: younger women with estrogen excess (obesity, estrogen without progesterone); looks like endometrium, less aggressive. Over 65 (70 to 80 on the slide): serous and clear cell endometrial carcinoma, not hormone-related, more aggressive. Over 60: the HPV-independent vulvar carcinoma from lichen sclerosus. Watch for: The estrogen-driven endometrioid type is the less aggressive one of younger women. Sarcoma botryoides is a little girls' tumor that does well when treated. Paget disease of the nipple (scaly, red): image the breast for the carcinoma beneath, which sets the prognosis. Leiomyoma: very common, benign, causes abnormal bleeding; leiomyosarcoma is aggressive, spreads to the lung.
